record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: What explains the gaps between the variance explained by concrete polygenic risk scores, SNP or genotype-based heritability, and twin-based heritability for complex human traits, and can those gaps be resolved by rare variants, non-additive genetic effects, gene-environment interactions, population structure, environmental bias, indirect genetic effects, improved prediction models, or a revised interpretation of heritability itself?

evidence.quote: the term “missing heritability” more commonly refers to the gap between heritability estimates from genotype and twin data [21].
Both of these inequalities reflect possible gaps in our understanding of the genetics of human traits (open problem #11: missing heritability).

Other explanations point out that SNP heritability could also be biased due to residual population structure [16, 21], environmental biases [62], indirect genetic effects [40] and genetic interactions (discussed later).

artifact.status_search_result: The missing-heritability gap remains an active and unresolved problem, but substantial progress has been made since 2021. Recent whole-genome-sequencing analyses and family-based designs have closed part of the SNP-vs-PRS gap (e.g., PRS for Alzheimer's, prostate cancer and type-2 diabetes now capture >75% of common-SNP heritability), and rare/structural variants plus indirect genetic effects have been shown to account for a meaningful fraction of the SNP-vs-twin gap. However, no single mechanism fully explains the gaps, and a complete decomposition into (a)–(h) is still lacking, so the problem is best characterized as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Finding missing heritability in complex traits
status_evidence.snippet: Common-variant heritability reaches only ∼40–50% for height, still below the ∼80% heritability estimated from twin studies; rare and structural variants and interactions remain candidate explanations.
status_evidence.claim: The gap between common-SNP heritability and twin heritability persists in 2025 but rare/structural variants are partially closing it.

status_evidence.title: Within- and Between-Family Validation of Nine Polygenic Risk Scores
status_evidence.snippet: Three PRS — Alzheimer's, prostate cancer, type-2 diabetes — explained over 75% of common-SNP heritability; within-family validation confirms substantial direct genetic effects.
status_evidence.claim: PRS now capture a large fraction of SNP heritability for some traits, narrowing the PRS-vs-SNP gap.

status_evidence.title: Highly parameterized polygenic scores tend to overfit to population stratification
status_evidence.snippet: Residual population stratification can inflate PRS performance and SNP-heritability estimates via random effects.
status_evidence.claim: Population structure remains a documented source of bias in heritability and PRS estimation.
